title: First Slug: Notes on Riding the Pulse for the First Time
body:
# First Slug: Notes on Riding the Pulse for the First Time

*Personal account submitted to the Vellichor Institute Mobility Studies archive. The author requested anonymity. Published with permission.*

## Zone 3 to Chicago Station

The Tier 4 sponsorship came through a research grant. Three years of fieldwork in the Gray Zone, a paper that Vellichor found interesting enough to fund, and a slot in a symposium in Rotterdam that required me to be there in person. The grant covered the slug ticket. I had never been inside Chicago Station.

I want to say that clearly, because people for whom Pulse transit is routine cannot imagine it: I had never been inside Chicago Station. I was born in Zone 3. I have lived in Zone 3 for thirty-one years. Chicago Station is in Zone 1, one kilometer from the building where I grew up, and I had never been inside it. The sponsorship credential loaded to my BCI at 0600 on a Tuesday. I walked to Zone 1 for the first time since a childhood errand I barely remember. The doors opened.

The station is underground. I had known this but had not understood it — the entrance is a descending atrium, glass and steel, and then you are below the city, in a space that is larger than the block above it and quieter than the street. The sound dampening is aggressive. After Zone 3, the silence felt like pressure.

## The Platform

The departure platform is not a platform in any sense I recognized. It is a pressurized chamber at the end of a long corridor that is clearly a section of Pulse tube — you can see the coil casings in the walls, the magnetic suspension rails, the inspection panels every forty meters. Then the corridor opens into the chamber, and the chamber is where passengers wait, seated in rows of reclined chairs that are already angled back at roughly thirty degrees.

A Ferrogate attendant explained the process to me because she noticed I was reading everything. The chairs recline further during the acceleration phase — the punch, she called it, matter-of-factly, the way you'd say 'the elevator' — and the correct response is to not grip anything. The GIDS field, she said, will be doing most of the work. It grabs your augments and pulls them forward with the slug. The remaining force goes through your seat. Gripping the armrests, she said, adds tension to muscles that are already being pulled in two directions and makes everything worse.

I asked what happened to unaugmented passengers.

She said: they feel it more. They're still fine. She said it in a way that indicated she had said this before.

## The Acceleration

The slug loaded in sections — cargo forward, passengers aft — through pressure-lock doors that sealed with a finality I felt in my chest. Then the doors sealed, and the external pressure equalized, and the hatch to the departure tube opened.

The punch was not what I had imagined. I had imagined something violent — a gun firing, a physical compression. What happened was this: a pressure developed in my back, gradual and even, like a very large hand pressing me gently and firmly into the reclined seat. My augments — the standard neural mesh, the BCI cluster behind my left ear, the reinforced cartilage in my knees from a Gray Zone accident two years ago — felt warm, briefly, and then the warmth was gone and the pressure was just pressure and I was watching the timer on the screen at the front of the cabin count up: 10 seconds, 20, 30.

At 47 seconds, the pressure stopped. The transition from acceleration to coasting was not a jolt — it simply ceased, the way a held note ends. We were at Mach 6. We were somewhere over Ohio, though 'over' is wrong because we were under the ground, in a vacuum tube, in the dark.

## Coasting

There is nothing to see. This is known and it is still disorienting.

The premium slug configuration includes screens showing camera feeds from the exterior of the slug — but there is no exterior, not in the way that matters. The cameras show the tube wall passing at a speed too high to resolve: a grey blur, and the coil sequence, and nothing else. Some passengers leave the screens on. I turned mine off after two minutes.

What I had instead: the low 8 Hz tick of the coil sequence, which I recognized immediately as the thrumline I had felt through my feet my entire life, and the knowledge that underneath that tick there was nothing — no air, no sound from outside, the Atlantic floor somewhere below if we were over the ocean yet, and we might be. The slug's position display said we were crossing 70°W longitude. That is somewhere over the North Atlantic.

I am a researcher who studies places. My entire professional life is about being somewhere and paying attention to it. I was nowhere. I was in a sealed cylinder at Mach 6 and there was nothing to pay attention to except other passengers who were reading or sleeping, and the timer on the screen, and the coil tick, and the fact that forty-three minutes is both a very short time and, in those conditions, a surprisingly long one.

I thought about my grandmother. She could hear the thrumline in our building. She thought it was the foundation settling. I had told her, years later, what it actually was. She had nodded slowly and said that explained a lot, and then she had said: *do they know we're here?* I had said yes, of course. The Pulse corridors are engineered around existing structures. Everything is surveyed.

She had looked at me with a patience I recognized as the patience of someone who is not asking a literal question.

## Rotterdam

The deceleration is the punch in reverse — nine kilometers of coil braking, the same gentle pressing force now from the front rather than the back. Then the pressure seals. Then a door.

I was in Rotterdam. It was raining. The transition from Chicago Station to Rotterdam Central had taken forty-three minutes, during which I had traveled 7,600 kilometers through a vacuum tube at Mach 6, felt nothing but the tick of the coils and the mild pressure of acceleration and deceleration, and thought about my grandmother.

Someone from Vellichor met me at the station exit with an umbrella. She said: first time?

I said: yes.

She said: does it feel like anything?

I said: it feels like being moved.
